rewrites.blindSummary:
A gubernatorial executive order (August 30, 2023) narrows the legal definitions of 'male' and 'female', declares a person's biological sex fixed at birth, ends state/province recognition of transgender people, and backs single-sex spaces for bathrooms and changing rooms - mostly resident-facing, but it signals an administration willing to use state/province machinery against gender identity.

The consequence axis is documented: the state/province houses trans prisoners by assigned birth sex in men's facilities — a transgender woman held in state/province custody (August 2022 national court ruling) was celled with a male sex offender who sexually assaulted her, and the court dismissed her failure-to-treat, surgery-denial and failure-to-protect claims, finding no deliberate indifference and no more than minimal injuries — so a trans woman in state/province custody faces birth-sex men's-prison placement with no proven judicial remedy against a violent cellmate.

Below the national score 0.36.
rewrites.blindTangential:
Legal observers recorded that opponents questioned the order's scope and legality when it was signed.

National framework turbulence: national prison guidelines allowed trans prisoners to be transferred to facilities matching their gender identity (January 2017) until they were rescinded on May 11, 2018, returning placement to sex assigned at birth — so the state/province's birth-sex practice matches the national guideline in force since 2018.

The August 2022 ruling is the state/province's only documented trans-prisoner case: a national district judge dismissed claims of failure to treat gender dysphoria, denial of gender-conforming surgery and failure to protect after the inmate was celled with a convicted sex offender who victimized her, writing that without medical evidence no reasonable jury could find deliberate indifference.

rewrites.blindSummary:
The state/province is the only state/province in the country with a standing criminal ban on gender-expressive performance: a 2023 adult entertainment statute criminalises 'adult cabaret entertainment' — defined to include 'male or female impersonators' — anywhere a child could see it, at up to 11 months 29 days and a $2,500 fine for a first offence and a 1–6 year felony on repeat. The ban is enforceable and current: the appeals court revived it on standing grounds and the nation's top court declined review (February 2025), so a visitor presenting in drag faces live charging exposure today rather than a dead-letter law.

The consequence axis reaches custody: under a 2026 women's safety-and-protection statute, transgender inmates are to be placed in prisons based on sex assigned at birth, and since April 2024 state/province law has banned gender-affirming care for inmates — so a trans visitor arrested here is housed by birth sex with no gender-affirming care allowed behind the walls.

For practical safety, killings of trans women run at 7.8 per 100k per year — above the general national homicide rate.
rewrites.blindTangential:
Adjacent litigation and policy flux: the nation's top court upheld the state/province's ban on gender-affirming care for minors in June 2025, and the drag ban's constitutionality has never been decided on the merits. A civil-liberties suit over a district attorney's threat to charge a 2023 Pride event also remains ongoing.

The adjacent provision of the same 2026 statute also bars trans women from women's shelters — a facility restriction beyond prisons attached to the same statute.
rewrites.blindLocalsOnly:
Since 2026 the state/province has also mandated birth-sex placement in prisons and shelters — a resident-facing facility practice.

The April 2024 in-prison ban on gender-affirming care governs the treatment of residents held in state/province custody.

rewrites.blindSummary:
The state/province operates one of the country's most actively enforced anti-trans regimes. Its facilities law (in force 4 December 2025) produced enforcement within days: state/province troopers checked identification at women's restrooms while cities and campuses adopted sharply divergent compliance and evasion policies, and the top government lawyer opened the first state/province bathroom-law enforcement inquiry of its kind — against a school district, escalated with a second records demand in April 2026 after a tip-line complaint.

The consequence axis reaches custody on two fronts: the facilities law expressly applies to prisons and other state/province government buildings — but on restroom use matching the sex on one's birth certificate, not on cell or facility assignment — while in a 2019 court ruling the state/province prison system denied a transgender inmate gender-confirmation surgery under its official policy, and the courts affirmed no deliberate indifference, treating the refusal as a permissible medical choice, leaving a trans person in state/province custody without a proven judicial remedy for denial of gender-affirming care.

Violence exposure is the national worst in absolute terms: 44 recorded killings of trans women over 2008–2025 (about 7.6 per 100k trans women per year; the monitoring project frames all rates as undercount floors). A July 2026 law-by-law legal-risk assessment grades the state/province in its top 'Do Not Travel' tier.
rewrites.blindTangential:
LGB-facing visibility is rolling back too: a city council rescinded its LGBTQ non-discrimination ordinance (Dec 2025) and a local Pride organisation suspended its 2026 events; a venue pulled out of a Pride event under school-board pressure.

Litigation flux: in the 2019 litigation, a national court denied the state/province's immunity defences but ruled against the transgender inmate on the Eighth Amendment claim, and the circuit court affirmed the dismissal (with a dissenting opinion on summary-judgement procedure) — documentation of the state/province's denial practice more than a change in it.
rewrites.blindLocalsOnly:

rewrites.blindSummary:
The nation under its current ruling movement is the most hostile environment on this map for a transgender person. A 2024 morality law obliges the regime's virtue police to prevent "homosexuality" and "lesbianism", including "even if with one's own spouse"; the ruling movement applies the death penalty for same-sex relations under its interpretation of religious law; and documented practice against LGBTIQ people includes beatings, sexual violence in detention, forced confessions, and house-to-house searches. Transgender residents report living in hiding, in windowless rooms, for years.

There is no legal recognition, no protection, no functioning consular protection, and no tourism infrastructure that would allow a visitor to blend in. A discovered trans visitor would face the same enforcement apparatus as local LGBTIQ people: detention with routine sexual and physical abuse of queer detainees, prosecution for moral crimes, and corporal punishment that international experts say is escalating into 2026.

The prison-housing axis is thin but must not read as neutral: nothing is documented on where trans prisoners are held — no birth-sex vs identity housing rule, no trans special units, no solitary or segregation practice — while an international human-rights organisation's report (January 2022, 60 interviews) documents wrongful-detention risk, threats, assault and blackmail of LGBTI people since the takeover; in a criminalising regime with no recourse, an undocumented placement practice means a detained trans visitor is held at the regime's discretion amid the documented abuse of queer detainees, not under any protected standard.

This is the reference point for the very bottom of the risk scale.
rewrites.blindTangential:
The applicable legal regime is layered and shifting: penal-code 'sodomy' provisions carry up to two years, while a religious-law reference clause permits the death penalty for same-sex activity and the 2024 morality law added surveillance duties; flogging documented by international experts nearly doubled in 2025 to at least 1,110 people.

Asylum-framework context: international guidance treats LGBTIQ people in the country as those perceived to transgress religious and social norms, and refugee-led organisations abroad document systematic persecution — context for the regime's treatment, not visitor-facing advice.

Enforcement context: the human-rights organisation's report (26 January 2022) records the ruling movement's members using leaked personal data to pursue individuals considered gay or gender-nonconforming, and it calls on the regime to end discrimination and violence against LGBTI people.
rewrites.blindLocalsOnly:
Resident-facing documentation: trans and gay residents report living in hiding, in windowless rooms, for years; family, neighbour and partner abuse surged after the 2021 takeover; security officials pursue gay men and trans women more systematically than in earlier rule.

Interview-based reports from residents in-country and abroad record physical and sexual assault, arbitrary detention and public flogging for alleged same-sex relations, with visibly transgender people facing the gravest risks including exploitation and violence.

A human-rights organisation's 26 January 2022 report (43 pages, 60 interviews with residents in-country and abroad) is the specific source base for those accounts of threats, assault, blackmail and wrongful-detention risk after the 15 August 2021 takeover; it describes no trans-prisoner placement practice at all.
rewrites.blindOutOfScope:
Armed conflict, terrorism, kidnapping, and the arbitrary detention of foreign nationals for leverage are severe risks for every visitor, independent of any personal characteristic.

Unresolved or unverifiable: enforcement figures rest on 2022-23 interview-based reports and 2025-26 international flogging counts rather than the regime's own statistics; most accounts predate the 2024 morality law's implementation, so current on-the-ground practice is inferred rather than directly documented; no tourist entry pathway exists to test in practice.

Prison-housing axis: there is no evidence at all on birth-sex vs identity placement, trans special units, or solitary/segregation practice — the only prison-relevant finding is general wrongful-detention danger; that gap is treated as danger here, because a regime that criminalises same-sex conduct and abuses queer detainees cannot be assumed to place trans prisoners safely.
